precepts.text: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much. This explains why Joseph was faithful. He's in slavery now, but he was faithful to Potiphar, and Potiphar raised him up. A lot of brothers and sisters have jobs; the Most High is observing us in whatever we're doing. The least that we're faithful in is these little jobs out here. Just like Joseph was in captivity, we're in captivity, but that doesn't mean we can steal, lie, or rob. When you're on your jobs, deal right. God is watching each and every one of us.
precepts.point: The Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. You notice the theme is the same: just like when Jacob worked for Laban all those years, Laban was blessed for Jacob's sake.
precepts.why:
Joseph was seventeen, a teenager, sold into Egypt: “Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmeelites.” Yet “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master “saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand,” and made him overseer over his house, putting all that he had into his hand.

Luke 16:10 explains why: “He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.” Joseph was in slavery, but he was faithful to Potiphar, and Potiphar raised him up.

It speaks to us today. Many brothers and sisters have jobs, and the Most High is observing us in whatever we do. The least that we are faithful in is these little jobs out here. Just as Joseph was in captivity, we are in captivity, but that does not mean we can steal, lie or rob. When you are on your jobs, do not steal; deal right. God is watching each and every one of us.

And look what faithfulness brought: “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake; and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.” The theme is the same as when Jacob worked for Laban all those years and Laban was blessed for Jacob’s sake. Faithful in little, Joseph was trusted with much, until his master “knew not ought he had, save the bread which he did eat.”

precepts.text: Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: that's what Joseph did. If thou comest too near it, it will bite thee. The teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men. If a snake fell in this room right now, everybody would be out of here. That snake is your sin.
precepts.point: Everybody's demon is not the same. For some it's food, but generally it's sexual demons that get the brothers. Take a page out of what our forefather Joseph did.
precepts.why:
Potiphar’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said, “Lie with me.” Joseph refused, and he did not refuse half-heartedly: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Notice he was not blaming God that he was a slave in a strange land. His master had kept nothing back from him “but thee, because thou art his wife,” and Joseph would not touch her.

This was not a single moment. “she spake to Joseph day by day”; she was trying to wear him down day by day. And the Egyptians loved beautiful women; remember when Abraham went down into Egypt, Sarah was in danger because of her beauty. Potiphar’s wife was no ugly woman; she was good on the eyes, and Joseph, at 17 years old, still said no. When she finally “caught him by his garment,” “he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.”

Sirach gives the precept for what Joseph did: “Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee: the teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men.” Joseph saw sin like a snake, and he ran like a rabbit. If a snake fell into the room right now, everybody would be out of there. That snake is your sin. “All iniquity is as a two edged sword, the wounds whereof cannot be healed.”

Everybody's demon is not the same. For some it is food; for most of the brothers it is sexual demons, and those demons will get you. Put yourself in Joseph's place and be honest about it: many have been put out for adultery two and three times. Take a page out of what our forefather Joseph did: don't stand there and reason with it, don't come near it. Flee.

precepts.text: A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many; strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men. Somebody that lies on you can do much destruction.
precepts.point: His master's wrath was kindled, and Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. Remember how old Joseph is: 17.
precepts.why:
When Potiphar’s wife could not get her way, she lied. She called the men of her house and said, “See, he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice.” Then “she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home”: she kept his clothes as false evidence, and told her husband the same lie.

Sirach shows what that kind of tongue does: “A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation: strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” Somebody that lies on you can do much destruction. Joseph was the greatest man in Potiphar's house, trusted with everything, and a lying tongue brought him down to the king's prison.

It is the same today. Many brothers have been locked up because a woman lied on them: an ex-wife or ex-girlfriend who wants his life to go down the tubes, who calls him over, is refused, and then threatens to tell the police he hurt her. Others are in jail because a woman started a fight and expected him to defend her. Don't deal with a woman like that; that is the kind of woman Joseph had over him.

And this same spirit met our people in slavery. A lot of us were put to death because of it. Emmett Till was put to death for the lying woman, and there are a lot of cases like that. What Potiphar's wife did to Joseph, a backbiting tongue has done to Israel again and again.

precepts.text: Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue. The tongue does a lot of evil, and that's what Potiphar's wife did to Joseph.
precepts.point: His master's wrath was kindled, and Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. Remember how old Joseph is: 17.
precepts.why:
Sirach goes on: “Many have fallen by the edge of the sword: but not so many as have fallen by the tongue.” The tongue does a lot of evil, and that is exactly what Potiphar’s wife did to Joseph. She never lifted a sword against him; she only spoke, and her words did the work.

She told her husband, “The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me,” and “when his master heard the words of his wife,” “his wrath was kindled.” On nothing but her word, “Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound.” Remember how old Joseph is here: 17.

That is how our people have fallen too: brothers in prison on a lie, and in slavery times men like Emmett Till put to death because of a lying woman's words. More have fallen by the tongue than by the sword. Guard yourself from the kind of company that can destroy you with a word.

precepts.text: My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation. Joseph understood this, because his father taught him. Make not haste in time of trouble: don't leave this truth in your time of trouble, because Satan will tell you that you had it better when you served him. Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate. Joseph's family was rich; Jacob was wealthy. Joseph was taken from all that, and now he's in the midst of poverty, in prison. Just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph.
precepts.point: His master's wrath was kindled, and Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. Remember how old Joseph is: 17.
precepts.why:
Joseph was 17, falsely accused, and thrown into the king's prison. Sirach tells you why this should not shock a servant of God: “My son, if thou come to serve the Lord, prepare thy soul for temptation.” Joseph understood this, because his father Jacob taught him.

“Set thy heart aright, and constantly endure, and make not haste in time of trouble.” Make not haste means don't leave this truth in your time of trouble. Satan will tell you, if you weren't in that Bible you wouldn't be going through half of what you're going through; you had it better when you served me. “Cleave unto him, and depart not away, that thou mayest be increased at thy last end.”

“Whatsoever is brought upon thee take cheerfully, and be patient when thou art changed to a low estate.” Joseph's family was rich; Jacob was a wealthy man. Joseph was taken from all that, sold as a slave, and now he is in the midst of poverty, in prison, for a crime he refused to commit. That is a low estate, and he bore it without leaving God.

Just as it goes for us, it went for our father Joseph. Israel today has been brought down to a low estate, and the tests and trials come because we serve the Lord. Endure them, cleave unto him, and you will be increased at your last end, as Joseph was.

precepts.text: When a man's ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him. That's what happened with Joseph.
precepts.point: But the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison. The keeper committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners; whatever Joseph did, the Lord made it to prosper.
precepts.why:
Even in prison, “the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.” The keeper “committed to Joseph’s hand all the prisoners that were in the prison,” and “looked not to any thing that was under his hand; because the Lord was with him, and that which he did, the Lord made it to prosper.”

Solomon gives the reason: “When a man’s ways please the Lord, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him.” That is what happened with Joseph. He was a Hebrew slave, accused of attacking his master's wife, locked in the place where the king's prisoners were bound, and his very jailer became favourable to him and handed him the whole prison.

It is the same pattern all through Joseph's life: in Potiphar's house the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house “for Joseph’s sake,” just as Laban was blessed for Jacob's sake when Jacob worked for him. Joseph's ways pleased the Lord; he refused sin even when it cost him, and whatever he did, the Lord made it to prosper. Keep your ways pleasing to God, and he will make even those set over you in captivity to be at peace with you.

precepts.text: Sit not at all with another man's wife; don't play with it. Don't be drinking around somebody else's wife, lest thine heart incline unto her, and through thy desire thou fall into destruction. Both of y'all are going to destroy everything.
precepts.point: Read on in Genesis 39: he end up going to prison behind this, because she lied on him.

note.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

precepts.why:
“the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master saw that the Lord was with him and made him overseer over his house, and “the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake.” And “Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured”: he had a very good reputation, and people looked at him as a man of integrity and good character.

Then his master’s wife “cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me.” He refused: his master had committed all that he had to his hand, “neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” Nobody was watching him. He could have done it, but he said no. That is where integrity comes from: making the right decision when nobody is watching.

Ecclesiasticus 9:9 gives the same wisdom as a command: “Sit not at all with another man’s wife, nor sit down with her in thine arms, and spend not thy money with her at the wine; lest thine heart incline unto her, and so through thy desire thou fall into destruction.” Do not sit with another man’s wife at all. Do not play with it. Do not be drinking around somebody else’s wife, because your heart will incline to her, and both of you will destroy everything.

Joseph lived that. When “there was none of the men of the house there within,” she caught him by his garment, “and he left his garment in her hand, and fled.” He knew it was wickedness that would destroy his reputation and everything he had worked so hard for, and that he would not only be sinning against her but against the Lord. He fled rather than sit with it, even though he went to prison when she lied on him.

precepts.text: Give them compassion before them who carried them captives; the Lord gave Joseph that compassion in Egypt.
precepts.point: The Most High deals with His people even in captivity and gives them compassion before them who carried them captive; the favor on Joseph is the pattern of that prayer.
precepts.why:
“And forgive thy people that have sinned against thee, and all their transgressions wherein they have transgressed against thee, and give them compassion before them who carried them captive, that they may have compassion on them.” That is the prayer for Israel in captivity, and the favor on Joseph is the pattern of it.

Joseph was carried captive, brought down to Egypt and bought by Potiphar out of the hands of the Ishmeelites. Yet “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man.” His master “saw that the Lord was with him”, Joseph “found grace in his sight”, and Potiphar made him overseer over his house and put all that he had into his hand. The Lord gave Joseph compassion before the man who held him.

The Most High deals with His people even in captivity. He blessed the Egyptian’s house for Joseph’s sake, “and the blessing of the Lord was upon all that he had in the house, and in the field.”

precepts.text: Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws; the laws are nothing new.
precepts.point: Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai. Abraham kept the commandments, statutes, and laws; and Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of the people might have lain with his wife and brought guiltiness upon them. The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt.
precepts.why:
“Because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.” Abraham kept the commandments, statutes and laws long before Sinai. The laws are nothing new.

That is how Joseph, generations before Moses, could call what Potiphar’s wife asked of him “this great wickedness” and “sin against God.” Adultery was known as sin from the beginning. Joseph knew the commandments his father’s fathers kept, and he refused.

precepts.text: Abimelech knew lightly lying with another man's wife would have brought guiltiness upon them; adultery was known sin.
precepts.point: Adultery was known as sin from the beginning, long before Sinai. Abraham kept the commandments, statutes, and laws; and Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of the people might have lain with his wife and brought guiltiness upon them. The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt.
precepts.why:
“And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lien with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us.” Abimelech rebuked Isaac because one of his people might have lain with Isaac’s wife, and that would have brought guiltiness upon them.

The nations themselves knew adultery brought guilt. If a heathen king knew it, Joseph surely knew it: lying with his master’s wife would be “this great wickedness”, and sin against God. So he refused her.

precepts.text: Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent; come too near and it will bite thee. Joseph fled.
precepts.point: That is the example: flee from sin as from the face of a serpent, for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee; the teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion. Joseph knew thirty more seconds of entertaining her would be the bite.
precepts.why:
“My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for thy former sins. Flee from sin as from the face of a serpent: for if thou comest too near it, it will bite thee: the teeth thereof are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men.”

That is exactly what Joseph did. She spake to him day by day and he hearkened not; then she arranged the empty house, caught him by his garment and said “Lie with me”, and “he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.” He did not stand and reason with her. He fled from sin as from the face of a serpent.

Joseph knew that thirty more seconds of entertaining her would be the bite. Come too near sin and it will bite thee, and its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men. That is the example: flee.

precepts.text: The woman whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands; whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her, as Joseph escaped.
precepts.point: The scriptures warn of that spirit: the woman whose heart is snares and nets and her hands as bands; whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her. The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, but her end is bitter, and her ways are moveable; the same mouth that flattered turns and accuses.
precepts.why:
“And I find more bitter than death the woman, whose heart is snares and nets, and her hands as bands: whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her; but the sinner shall be taken by her.” Potiphar’s wife was that woman. Her heart was snares and nets, laid day by day, and her hands were bands: she caught him by his garment.

Joseph pleased God, and he escaped from her. She was left with his garment in her hand, and the sinner would have been taken; but he fled. Then the same woman turned and lied, crying that “he hath brought in an Hebrew unto us to mock us”, and laid up his garment by her as evidence until his lord came home. That is the spirit the scriptures warn of.

precepts.text: The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, but her end is bitter as wormwood; her ways are moveable.
precepts.point: The scriptures warn of that spirit: the woman whose heart is snares and nets and her hands as bands; whoso pleaseth God shall escape from her. The lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, but her end is bitter, and her ways are moveable; the same mouth that flattered turns and accuses.
precepts.why:
“For the lips of a strange woman drop as an honeycomb, and her mouth is smoother than oil: But her end is bitter as wormwood, sharp as a twoedged sword.” The lips that said “Lie with me” day by day were smooth as oil; the end of it was bitter as wormwood. “Her feet go down to death; her steps take hold on hell.”

“her ways are moveable, that thou canst not know them.” The same mouth that flattered Joseph turned and accused him: “The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me.” She moved from wanting him to destroying him, holding his garment as proof. That is what a strange woman is, and that is why Joseph was right to flee her.

precepts.text: Jealousy is the rage of a man; he will not spare in the day of vengeance nor regard any ransom; that is why no plea could reach Potiphar.
precepts.point: When his master heard the words of his wife, his wrath was kindled and he put Joseph into the prison. He did not seek understanding, for jealousy is the rage of a man: he will not spare in the day of vengeance, nor regard any ransom.
precepts.why:
“For jealousy is the rage of a man: therefore he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not regard any ransom; neither will he rest content, though thou givest many gifts.” That is why no plea could reach Potiphar. When he heard the words of his wife, “his wrath was kindled”, and he put Joseph into the prison where the king’s prisoners were bound. He did not seek understanding; jealousy is the rage of a man.

The same place shows what adultery would have cost Joseph had he done it: “whoso committeth adultery with a woman lacketh understanding: he that doeth it destroyeth his own soul. A wound and dishonour shall he get; and his reproach shall not be wiped away.” Joseph refused the sin and still got the prison, because a jealous man will not spare in the day of vengeance nor regard any ransom.

precepts.text: The fetters and the iron of the psalm are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.
precepts.point: The famine itself was called by the Most High, and the man was sent before them, even Joseph, sold for a servant, whose feet they hurt with fetters. The fetters and the iron are the prison where the king's prisoners were bound.

note.label: Genesis 45: Joseph Made Known unto His Brethren

precepts.why:
“And Joseph’s master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king’s prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison.” The fetters and the iron of the psalm are this prison, the place where the king’s prisoners were bound.

That was part of the Most High sending him before them. From that prison Joseph went on to become a father to Pharaoh and lord of all his house, to preserve his brethren a posterity in the earth.

precepts.text: The Most High was with Joseph and made him overseer over the house of his Egyptian master.
precepts.point: The king loosed him and made him lord of his house and ruler of his substance, to bind his princes and teach his senators wisdom. Our forefather Joseph taught the Egyptians; those who boast in Egyptology forget our forefathers taught them.

note.label: Psalm 105: Remember His Marvelous Works from Abraham to the Exodus

precepts.why:
“He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant”. Genesis shows the Most High with him in that servitude: “the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; and he was in the house of his master the Egyptian.”

“And his master saw that the Lord was with him, and that the Lord made all that he did to prosper in his hand. And Joseph found grace in his sight, and he served him: and he made him overseer over his house, and all that he had he put into his hand.” The Egyptian master himself saw that the Lord was with Joseph and put everything he had into his hand.

This is the beginning of what the psalm ends with: the king loosed him and “made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance”, to bind his princes at his pleasure “and teach his senators wisdom.” Our forefather Joseph taught the Egyptians. Those who boast in Egyptology forget that our forefathers taught them.

moments.label: Character & Integrity: The Hidden Strength Behind Wisdom

points: The modern day Satan kisses are today's traps, and the pattern holds through all the examples: Eve engaged, rationalized, and fell into idolatry. Samson was compromised and lost his strength. David looked, acted on it, and brought judgment on his family. Judas chased money and destroyed himself; money was his demise. Joseph fled immediately, and the Lord promoted him with blessings. Sometimes you pray, Lord take this away from me, and then immediately you get put in a situation to prove yourself on the very thing you asked him to take away. Recognize the test when it comes.

This is the example of what to do when you are in the confined space, when your back is against the wall. Joseph had everything in his favor: the Lord was with him, his master saw the Lord made all he did prosper, and he was made overseer over the house.

And it came to pass after these things, that his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me. Satan had to come in: it is too good in here, you got promoted, the Lord is with you; I have to test you now.

But he refused. He said, my master has trusted me with everything in this house, and he has kept back nothing from me but thee, because thou art his wife. You are off limits. Joseph is reasoning; he is painting the picture: the Lord gave me favor to be in this position.

How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? This is a person that immediately resisted the devil. He did not have to think; that lets you know the scripture was always in his mind. Easy decision, no negotiation, no emotional engagement whatsoever. And you know Pharaoh's officer's wife was attractive; Joseph did not care about any of that.

Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, captain of the guard, an Egyptian, bought him of the hands of the Ishmaelites. And the Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man; his master saw that the Lord was with him, and made him overseer over his house.
The Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. You notice the theme is the same: just like when Jacob worked for Laban all those years, Laban was blessed for Jacob's sake.

She spake to Joseph day by day; she was trying to wear him down day by day. And remember, the Egyptians loved beautiful women; when Abraham went down, Sarah was in danger because of her beauty. Potiphar's wife was not bad looking, and Joseph still said no.

His master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph, and she said, lie with me. But he refused: there is none greater in this house than I, neither hath he kept back anything from me but thee, because thou art his wife. How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? Notice Joseph wasn't blaming God that he was in slavery.
She caught him by his garment, saying, lie with me; and he left his garment in her hand, and fled. Put yourself in Joseph's place at 17 years old. He saw sin like a snake and he ran like a rabbit.

She called unto the men of her house and said, he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice. She couldn't get her way, so she lied. And she laid up his garment by her until his lord came home; she kept his clothes as false evidence.
His master's wrath was kindled, and Joseph's master took him and put him into the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were bound. Remember how old Joseph is: 17.

But the Lord was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison. The keeper committed to Joseph's hand all the prisoners; whatever Joseph did, the Lord made it to prosper.
The Lord was with Joseph, and he was a prosperous man. His master saw that the Lord was with him and made him overseer over his house, and the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake.
